candidate.proposed_limit: Nongeometric L-functions and the absence of a classical cohomology model show that direct transplantation of the finite-field proof is incomplete.
candidate.title: Index-theorem route and its boundary

parents.title: RH becomes negativity of an explicit-formula quadratic form

accepted_interpretation.interpretation: Within the visible boundary, RH is recast as a uniform negativity requirement over a restricted family built from g, rather than as separate assertions about individual zeros. The finite-field case supplies a comparison mechanism: an algebraic index theorem forces negative semidefiniteness of the self-intersection form on degree-zero divisors. This gains a structural sign target and shows how geometry can force the analogous sign, but it does not identify the missing classical right-hand side or establish a transfer from divisor intersections to the classical problem. The remaining burden is to recover the omitted quadratic expression from a wider span and prove its negativity for every admissible function, with the two vanishing-integral constraints, the function class W, and the sign convention intact.
accepted_interpretation.nonparaphrase_operation: Abstracts only the source-visible common proof obligation—a sign condition—and compares an asserted classical uniform-negativity criterion with a geometrically forced finite-field sign, while auditing which part of the classical representation is absent.
accepted_interpretation.quality_reason: Accepted as a bounded structural interpretation because the test-function restrictions, equivalence claim, and finite-field intersection-form mechanism are explicit. Its use is deliberately limited: the unit begins mid-reference and cannot support an exact reconstruction of the classical right-hand side.
accepted_interpretation.source_support: The span claims equivalence between RH and negativity of an already-referenced right-hand side for all displayed convolution-type f built from g∈W satisfying ∫g(x)dx/x=0 and ∫g(x)dx=0. It then states that, for curves over finite fields, the analogous negativity follows from the algebraic index theorem, whose visible statement makes divisor self-intersection negative semidefinite on degree-zero divisors.
accepted_interpretation.speculation_status: The identification of the omitted right-hand side with a prime-side explicit formula is withheld. The displayed product/convolution may have extraction damage, and any exact classical quadratic criterion or geometric transfer claim requires a wider source span or scan check.

parents.title: Random-matrix spectra point toward a missing classical cohomology, Frobenius, and index theorem

accepted_interpretation.interpretation: The analogy is useful when it predicts structural obligations rather than merely matching distributions. It suggests that self-adjointness or geometric negativity could explain zero location, while the nongeometric cases indicate that the sought structure may need a broader form.
accepted_interpretation.nonparaphrase_operation: Spacing correlations bridge L-function zeros to random-matrix eigenvalues; finite-field cohomology and Frobenius provide a working model for how spectral data can arise from geometry.
accepted_interpretation.quality_reason: The source connects zero-spacing correlations to orthogonal, unitary, and symplectic random-matrix limits, mentions Hilbert-Polya, contrasts the unconditional finite-field theory, and explicitly asks for cohomology, Frobenius, and index-theorem analogues. The output correctly marks these global structures as questions and Maass L-functions as a boundary of a purely geometric analogy.
accepted_interpretation.source_support: Bombieri connects zero-spacing work with orthogonal, unitary, and symplectic random-matrix limits and with the Hilbert–Pólya proposal of a self-adjoint operator. He contrasts this heuristic with Katz–Sarnak's unconditional finite-field theory and asks for classical analogues of cohomology, Frobenius, and an index theorem.
accepted_interpretation.speculation_status: Matching local statistics does not construct an operator or prove RH. The proposed global structures are explicitly questions, and Maass L-functions mark a concrete limit of a purely geometric transfer. This unit is deliberately speculative; only the cited correlations and finite-field comparison are presented as established background. Saying a useful analogy supplies structural obligations rather than merely a distributional match is a reasonable conceptual interpretation. The source itself labels the global discussion conjectural and speculative; the output preserves that epistemic status.
